metadata.file_name: Combining statistical and machine learning methods to explore German students  attitudes towards ICT in PISA.pdf
metadata.title: Combining statistical and machine learning methods to explore German students’ attitudes towards ICT
metadata.venue: International Journal of Research & Method in Education

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 German student questionnaire data with an additional optional ICT familiarity questionnaire. The analytic samples were restricted by removing cases with 100% missing ICT responses (ICT questionnaire optional in Germany), yielding N=5411 (2015) and N=4507 (2018) from 254 and 208 German schools, respectively. The paper does not report applying PISA sampling weights (e.g., student/school weights) in the RF or HLM analyses; instead, it focuses on model-based estimation and multilevel structure, and it uses Fay’s method with 80 replicates for sampling variance in the HLM with plausible values. Because the manuscript does not name any weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and does not describe weighted estimation for the RF steps, the weighting strategy is not fully transparent for the ML components.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used German subsets of PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 student questionnaire and the optional ICT familiarity questionnaire. Removed cases with 100% missing ICT responses due to the ICT questionnaire being optional in Germany (1093 cases removed in 2015; 944 cases removed in 2018). For RF classification, used an 80% training split of the 2015 sample (with oversampling of the training set to address class imbalance) and evaluated on the remaining 20% test split; for RF performance on 2018, evaluated on the full 2018 dataset. For HLM, built models for mathematical and scientific literacy using 10 plausible values and included gender, ESCS, and four ICT attitude indices simultaneously; random-intercept models were used because random slopes failed to converge.

main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics proficiency level (below Level 2, Levels 2–4, Level 5+)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (multiclass AUC): 67.44% on the 2015 test set (20% hold-out). When evaluated on 2018 data: multiclass AUC = 69.19%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Germany) the study leveraged ESCS, ICT autonomy, gender, ICT interest, and ICT competence to predict mathematics proficiency level categories, finding that ICT autonomy was among the most important ICT attitudes for classification and that higher autonomy increased the probability of higher proficiency classes. This indicates that strengthening students’ ICT autonomy may be a promising lever for improving mathematics achievement distributions, though the study is cross-sectional and predictive performance does not establish causality.

main_findings.target_variable: Science proficiency level (below Level 2, Levels 2–4, Level 5+)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (multiclass AUC): 71.66% on the 2015 test set (20% hold-out). When evaluated on 2018 data: multiclass AUC = 68.51%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Germany) the study leveraged ESCS, ICT autonomy, gender, ICT interest, and ICT in social interaction to predict science proficiency level categories, finding that ICT autonomy was the most important ICT attitude and that higher autonomy increased the probability of Level 5+ while higher ICT in social interaction increased the probability of below Level 2. This indicates that ICT autonomy-focused interventions may support stronger science achievement profiles, while social-interaction-oriented ICT engagement may require careful interpretation, given the predictive (not causal) design.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (Germany) Mathematics literacy (10 plausible values; continuous scale)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematical literacy score (PVs combined via plausible values with Fay replicates)
main_findings.performance_metrics: HLM fixed effects (2015): ICT in social interaction β = −10.76 (p < .001); ICT autonomy β = 22.56 (p < .001). Nakagawa R²: marginal = .055, conditional = .444.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Germany) the study leveraged gender, ESCS, and four ICT attitude indices to model mathematical literacy scores with a random-intercept HLM, finding that ICT autonomy had a significant positive association with mathematics literacy while ICT in social interaction had a significant negative association and ICT competence/interest were not significant at the .001 level. This indicates that policies and classroom practices that build students’ independent control over ICT use may align with higher mathematics literacy, though the cross-sectional associations cannot be interpreted as causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (Germany) Science literacy (10 plausible values; continuous scale)
main_findings.target_variable: Scientific literacy score (PVs combined via plausible values with Fay replicates)
main_findings.performance_metrics: HLM fixed effects (2015): ICT in social interaction β = −14.33 (p < .001); ICT autonomy β = 38.29 (p < .001). Nakagawa R²: marginal = .066, conditional = .444.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Germany) the study leveraged gender, ESCS, and four ICT attitude indices to model scientific literacy scores with a random-intercept HLM, finding that ICT autonomy was the strongest positive ICT attitude (β = 38.29, p < .001) while ICT in social interaction was significantly negative (β = −14.33, p < .001) and ICT competence/interest were not significant at the .001 level. This indicates that fostering ICT autonomy may be particularly relevant for science learning outcomes, but the evidence remains correlational due to the observational PISA design.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Germany) Mathematics literacy (10 plausible values; continuous scale)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematical literacy score (PVs combined via plausible values with Fay replicates)
main_findings.performance_metrics: HLM fixed effects (2018): ICT in social interaction β = −9.21 (p < .001); ICT autonomy β = 17.45 (p < .001). Nakagawa R²: marginal = .055, conditional = .408.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Germany) the study leveraged gender, ESCS, and four ICT attitude indices to model mathematical literacy scores with a random-intercept HLM, finding that ICT autonomy remained significantly positively associated with mathematics literacy and ICT in social interaction remained significantly negatively associated, while other ICT attitudes were not significant at the .001 threshold. This indicates that the ICT autonomy–achievement association is relatively stable across PISA waves, supporting the case for sustained ICT autonomy development rather than one-off initiatives.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Germany) Science literacy (10 plausible values; continuous scale)
main_findings.target_variable: Scientific literacy score (PVs combined via plausible values with Fay replicates)
main_findings.performance_metrics: HLM fixed effects (2018): ICT in social interaction β = −21.08 (p < .001); ICT autonomy β = 25.99 (p < .001). Nakagawa R²: marginal = .057, conditional = .411.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Germany) the study leveraged gender, ESCS, and four ICT attitude indices to model scientific literacy scores with a random-intercept HLM, finding that ICT autonomy was significantly positively associated with science literacy (β = 25.99, p < .001) and ICT in social interaction was significantly negative (β = −21.08, p < .001), with ICT competence/interest not significant at the .001 level in the reported models. This indicates that ICT autonomy may be a robust correlate of science achievement across time, suggesting that education systems should consider autonomy-supportive ICT practices when designing digital learning strategies.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes German PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 student data, focusing on attitudes toward ICT (ICT competence, ICT interest, ICT in social interaction, ICT autonomy) and their relationship to mathematics and science literacy. For missing data imputation and for predicting proficiency level categories (below Level 2, Levels 2–4, Level 5+), it uses Random Forest with RF-based imputation (missForest) and multiclass AUC evaluation: mathematics AUC = 67.44% (2015 test) and 69.19% (2018), science AUC = 71.66% (2015 test) and 68.51% (2018). For associations with continuous literacy scores, it fits random-intercept HLM using 10 plausible values and Fay’s method (80 replicates), finding ICT autonomy significantly positive and ICT in social interaction significantly negative in both years. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference), potential transparency gaps about survey-weight application for ML steps, and the fact that predictive importance does not equal causal effects.
